object_types.name: Incident
object_types.definition: An event declared when something breaks, requiring investigation, mitigation, and resolution. Identified by a unique incident number.

source_references.excerpt: How is an incident identified? ... Incident number. INC-, then a sequence.
Something breaks. We find out about it, one way or another. Somebody declares an incident, somebody runs it, we fix it, we write it up.

object_types.name: IncidentNumber
object_types.definition: The unique identifier for an incident, formatted as INC- followed by a sequence number.

source_references.excerpt: Incident number. INC-, then a sequence. ... Unique. And we never delete incidents, which becomes relevant later.

object_types.name: Alert
object_types.definition: A notification generated by the monitoring platform or raised manually by an engineer when a system issue is detected.

source_references.excerpt: Monitoring fires an alert, or a customer tells us.
If an engineer spots something, they raise it, and raising it creates an alert record. It's a manual alert but it's still an alert.

object_types.name: AlertId
object_types.definition: The unique identifier for an alert, provided by the monitoring platform.

source_references.excerpt: And an alert -- identified how? ... Alert ID. Comes from the monitoring platform.

object_types.name: Ticket
object_types.definition: A customer support ticket reporting a problem. Some tickets are converted into incidents.

source_references.excerpt: And a ticket has a ticket number. Different system, different format, always has.
The alert fires and support gets three tickets in the same two minutes.

object_types.name: TicketNumber
object_types.definition: The unique identifier for a ticket in the support system.

source_references.excerpt: And a ticket has a ticket number. Different system, different format, always has.

object_types.name: Severity
object_types.definition: A classification of incident impact based on blast radius and technical severity.

source_references.excerpt: Now, severity. Nadia? ... SEV1 through SEV4. It's about blast radius and technical impact. SEV1 is everything's down for everyone. SEV4 is degraded, cosmetic, one region, nobody's really suffering.

object_types.name: Priority
object_types.definition: A classification of incident urgency based on business impact, customer urgency, and SLA consequences.

source_references.excerpt: And priority is P1 through P4. ... Priority is about customer urgency. Who's affected, what they've promised their own customers, whether we're breaching an SLA.

object_types.name: IncidentState
object_types.definition: The current stage of an incident: triage, declared, mitigated, resolved, or closed.

source_references.excerpt: What are the states? ... Triage, declared, mitigated, resolved, closed. ... Exactly one at a time.

object_types.name: Person
object_types.definition: An individual who can serve as an incident commander.

source_references.excerpt: The incident commander. One person, named, and it's a role for the duration, not a job title.

object_types.name: PersonId
object_types.definition: A unique identifier for a person.

source_references.excerpt: The incident commander. One person, named, and it's a role for the duration, not a job title.

object_types.name: Service
object_types.definition: A software service or system component owned by a team. An incident affects one or more services.

source_references.excerpt: And an incident affects a service? ... One or more. Usually one, sometimes several when it's an infrastructure thing. How is a service identified? ... Service name. They're unique, we enforce it in the catalogue.

object_types.name: ServiceName
object_types.definition: The unique name identifying a service.

source_references.excerpt: Service name. They're unique, we enforce it in the catalogue.

object_types.definition: A group that owns a service. The service owner is a team, not an individual.

source_references.excerpt: Is a service owner a team or a person? ... A team. Services are owned by teams. People move.

ambiguities.description: Commander mandatory scope unclear: The rule states 'declared incidents have exactly one commander; triage incidents have none.' However, the constraint is applied globally in the model. The system needs to enforce mandatory commander presence only for incidents in the 'declared' state. This is a temporal/state-dependent constraint that may require additional modeling (e.g., a subset constraint between 'Incident is in IncidentState(declared)' and 'Incident is commanded by Person'). Today's model captures the textual rule but may not fully prevent violation when implementing in a relational database.

source_references.excerpt: An incident starts in triage. In triage there's no commander, that's the point of triage: someone's looking at whether this is even real. A commander is assigned when it's declared. ... Declared incidents have exactly one commander. Triage incidents have none.

ambiguities.description: Person identification scheme: The model assigns 'person_id' as the reference mode for Person entities, but the transcript does not specify how persons are uniquely identified in the system. Candidates could include employee ID, name, email, or another identifier. This should be clarified with the team.

source_references.excerpt: The incident commander. One person, named, and it's a role for the duration, not a job title.

ambiguities.description: Team identification scheme: Similar to Person, the model assigns 'team_id' as the reference mode for Team entities. The transcript does not specify the actual identifier used (e.g., team name, team number, code). This should be clarified.

source_references.excerpt: Is a service owner a team or a person? ... A team. Services are owned by teams. People move.

ambiguities.description: Duplicate chain prevention: The transcript states that duplicate chains 'shouldn't' occur and are 'wrong' when they undercoun incidents in reports, but notes that 'nothing stops you making a chain' and they are 'not enforced today.' The model captures this as an acyclic ring constraint with medium confidence, but the rule is aspirational rather than actively enforced. Implementation will require explicit validation logic.

source_references.excerpt: Can a chain form? B duplicates A, C duplicates B? ... It shouldn't. The intent is that everything points at the primary directly. But nothing stops you making a chain and I've seen two-deep ones. ... So duplicates should point directly at a primary, and a primary is not itself a duplicate of anything. That's the rule as intended. It's not enforced.

ambiguities.description: Customer-caused incident classification: A significant discussion arises about whether incidents later determined to be caused by customer misconfiguration should be reclassified, excluded from reliability metrics, or left unchanged. The team does not reach a decision; the issue is escalated to Ravi (presumably leadership). The current model does not include a cause classification field or exclusion status. A future decision may require extending the model to capture this.

source_references.excerpt: Is there a decision here today? ... No, and it's above all three of us. That's a decision about what we report to the board, and Ravi owns that. ... Parking it explicitly, then. Whether an incident later found to be caused by customer misconfiguration should be reclassified, excluded from reliability metrics, or left as-is, is undecided. The model today captures the five states and does not include any concept of a cause classification, because there isn't one to capture.

ambiguities.description: Severity and priority change tracking: The transcript mentions that severity is 'constantly' revised during an incident as understanding of blast radius improves, and changes are recorded 'as events' in the incident timeline. However, the model captures only the current severity and priority, not the historical timeline. The facilitator explicitly notes 'I'll model the current one and note that changes exist in the timeline,' accepting this limitation. Future requirements may call for modeling historical severity/priority versions.

source_references.excerpt: Can either change during the incident? ... Constantly. Severity gets revised as we understand the blast radius. That's normal and expected. ... In the timeline, as events. The incident record carries the current severity. I'll model the current one and note that changes exist in the timeline.

ambiguities.description: Monitoring system integration: The transcript references a monitoring platform that fires alerts and a separate support ticketing system. The model treats Alert and Ticket as independent entities, but does not capture the relationship between the monitoring system, the support system, and the incident management system. The nature of integration (real-time, batch, manual reconciliation) is unclear.

source_references.excerpt: Monitoring fires an alert, or a customer tells us. ... The alert fires and support gets three tickets in the same two minutes.

ambiguities.description: Service catalogue governance: Services are identified by name and described as 'unique' and 'enforced in the catalogue,' but the transcript does not specify who maintains the catalogue, how names are assigned, or whether a service must exist in the catalogue before being linked to an incident. This governance aspect is out of scope for the current model but is relevant for implementation.

source_references.excerpt: How is a service identified? ... Service name. They're unique, we enforce it in the catalogue.
